abstract: |
  A study's protocol, experiment script, analysis pipeline, and manuscript figures all begin as views of one design. They drift apart as the study runs, until no artifact describes the study as it was actually run. What is missing is a record of the *process*. Cognitive science has mature standards for its data, such as BIDS; the process that produced the data still lives in scattered text, slides, and custom code. We present *Studyflow*, a visual notation that gives the experimental process one machine-readable, human-understandable, and executable representation. A study is represented as a typed directed graph, realized as an extension of the Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN 2.0) with the elements experimental research in cognitive science needs: domain-specific activities (cognitive task, questionnaire, instruction), decision gateways (randomization, eligibility), data operations, and data elements bound to community standards. One Studyflow diagram is at once the protocol, the runnable study, the analysis specification, and the publication figure, projected as multiple views for different audiences. We demonstrate the notation end to end with a benchmark experiment: a cohort of artificial agents performs a battery of cognitive tasks over many runs from one studyflow diagram, while the same file administers human participants behind one interface. One registrable file enrolls, runs, and analyzes artificial agents and people.
impact-statement: |
  A single machine-readable diagram serves as a study's protocol, runnable experiment, analysis specification, and publication figure for both human participants and artificial agents.

# Introduction

## The reproducibility gap is in *processes*, not just data

Every experimental study accumulates documents that describe it, and by the end they usually disagree. A study passes through many hands, human and automated, each leaving its own description: it is designed, approved, run, ingested, trained on, reviewed as a manuscript, and rebuilt by a replicator, and nothing keeps these descriptions consistent. Recovering what was actually run, let alone reproducing it, requires more than the data and the manuscript; it requires an explicit, complete description of the *processes* that generated them [@aguilar2022experiments; @momeni2026guidelines]. This is a general property of computing systems: a complete description needs both a data model (for structure and inputs/outputs) and a process model (for behavior) [@olive2007conceptual].

In cognitive sciences, the processes behind the data are documented mainly in narrative prose, ad hoc lab conventions, box-and-arrow diagrams, or code repositories [@bell2021perspectives; @osc2015; @nosek2022replicability]. The community has strong standards for the data, notably BIDS; the process, a record of how those data came to be, has no equivalent. This asymmetry has measurable consequences: even articles that share open data cannot easily be reproduced, because the process connecting the data to the results stays informal [@cruwell2023badge].

The cost of this missing process model is clearest when someone other than the author reads a study. A task battery, an online study, or an AI benchmark each accumulates the same trail: the protocol PDF, the ethics application, the experiment script, the preprocessing notebook, the model card [@mitchell2019modelcards], the manuscript figure, and the participant flow diagram. All begin as views of the same study and all end inconsistent. An inter-stimulus interval fixed at 500 ms in the protocol ships as 450 ms in the script, rounds to about half a second in the methods text, and vanishes from the figure caption; four artifacts disagree about one number and none is authoritative. That example is hypothetical, but the divergence it depicts is measured at every stage. Auditing every trial in five leading medical journals, @goldacre2019compare found only nine of 67 reported their outcomes faithfully. Re-running the analyses behind a mandatory open-data policy, @hardwicke2018cognition reproduced every target value without author help in only 11 of 35 articles, and 13 failed even after the authors helped. When the analysis is re-specified rather than re-run, independent teams diverge sharply: 29 teams on one question spanned odds ratios from 0.89 to 2.93 [@silberzahn2018manyanalysts], and 70 teams on one neuroimaging dataset produced no two identical workflows [@botviniknezer2020variability]. By the time anyone but the author reads the study, no single artifact describes it *as it was actually run*, and divergence among the artifacts bounds how far reviewers and replications can trust the code and data.

The usual compensation for a missing process model is voluntary narrative reporting: checklists, preregistration forms, and journal endorsements. The available evidence suggests it has limited effect. A 2022 survey of 400 psychology articles found only 7-14% preregistered and 14-16% sharing raw data, the lower bounds from a broad sample and the upper from prominent journals [@hardwicke2024prevalence]. Despite a decade of reform, gaps between endorsement and adherence recur across fields and journal policies [@percie2020arrive; @hair2019iicarus; @hardwicke2024transparency]. This is not a compliance failure but a structural one. A checklist records *what to mention* without requiring *what to share*, accepting a narrative of a process in place of a formal, verifiable one. Even preregistration, the strongest of these instruments, fixes a static plan. That plan cannot track the adaptive designs and data-dependent decisions of contemporary studies, and the gap between registered plan and executed procedure reopens the moment the study deviates [@claesen2021adherence; @hardwicke2023preregistration]. This is not limited to human research. The sibling field of AI evaluation has reached the same state. A benchmark is an experiment, and no current artifact records its procedure (see "Related work"). The underlying process model stays implicit, and implicit means open to interpretation.

We argue that reproducibility should be a property of the shared artifact, not separate documentation kept alongside the work. That artifact is a single living representation, machine-readable and human-understandable, that keeps the process model and the data model aligned across a study's many audiences. We pursue one version of that idea here, built on a standard process notation.

This paper makes three contributions. First, *Studyflow*, a notation that turns the experimental process into one artifact: a single file that is at once the protocol, the runnable study, the analysis specification, and the publication figure, realized as a domain-specific extension of BPMN 2.0 and projected as multiple views. Second, a formal account of that artifact, a typed directed graph with explicit validity conditions, view projections, and stated limits on what it can express, together with open-source tooling to author and execute Studyflow diagrams. Third, an example study run end to end from a single file: a benchmark that profiles a cohort of artificial agents across a battery of cognitive tasks, accompanied by human data that the same file collects behind one interface.

## Related work

Existing approaches to process representation fall into a few overlapping families that separate along two axes, whether a representation is for definition or for execution, and whether it is domain-generic or domain-specific: workflow engines and DSLs are executable but generic and code friendly; reporting guidelines and data standards are domain-specific but descriptive; visual notations are readable but rarely executable. None occupies the subspace we target here, a domain-specific notation that is at once a readable definition and an executable specification; we summarize the families, leaving more details to Supplementary Note 2.

*Workflow engines* represent analysis as a directed acyclic graph and run it at scale (Galaxy, KNIME, Nextflow, Snakemake, NiPype, the Common Workflow Language) [@thegalaxycommunity2024; @berthold2009; @nextflow; @wirth2024; @cwl; @pydra], but their representations target machines and developers, fit fixed data pipelines, and encode study logic in code [@peikert2021reproducible].

*Orchestration platforms* specify and run the experiment itself using presentation libraries (PsychoPy, jsPsych, lab.js, Gorilla) [@peirce2019psychopy; @deleeuw2015jspsych; @henninger2022labjs; @anwylirvine2020gorilla], online tools (oTree, Empirica, PsyNet) [@chen2016otree; @almaatouq2021empirica; @harrison2026psynet], code that compiles stimulus descriptions for humans or computers (SweetPea, AutoRA, SweetBean) [@musslick2022sweetpea; @musslick2024autora; @strittmatter2025sweetbean], and trial state machines (BEADL) [@beadl]. Each specifies one slice, a stimulus sequence, a trial, or a deployment; none spans the many steps of an experimental study (protocols, eligibility criteria, allocation, analysis, data formats, and the published figure) as one artifact.

*Guidelines and protocol registries* share protocols as custom text (protocols.io) and catalog reporting guidelines (e.g., CONSORT, SPIRIT, STROBE, PRISMA) [@teytelman2016; @simera2010equator; @hopewell2025consort; @chan2025spirit; @strobe; @page2021prisma], enforcing structure only at reporting time, in prose and PDF. Executable publishing makes the analysis narrative runnable but still leaves the experimental procedure as text [@maciocci2019era; @lakens2021machinereadable].

*Data standards and ontologies* (BIDS, Psych-DS, CSVW, Behaverse Data Model, the FAIR principles) [@bids; @psychds; @csvw; @bdm; @fair] make the data machine-readable but say little about the process that produced it.

*Provenance and packaging* (W3C PROV, RO-Crate, Workflow Run RO-Crate, process mining) [@w3cprov; @soilandreyes2022rocrate; @leo2024wfrunrocrate; @vanderaalst2016process] describe what was run retrospectively, not a prospective executable specification. They track the computational graph but leave the experimental graph (who was eligible, how they were allocated, and why a trial was excluded) only partially recorded. The Studyflow notation we develop here is complementary, and these standards can package its runs (see Discussion).

*Visual notations* communicate at a glance but are rarely standardized or tied to code [@bogale2024]; BPMN [@bpmnspec], already extended into domain profiles for clinical pathways and machine learning [@braun2014; @tetzlaff2022bpmn4sml], and Systems Biology Graphical Notation [@novere2009] show the need for domain-specific graphical formalization, yet none targets experimental cognitive science with all its particularities (experimental design, data collection, complex pipelines, and the need to serve human and machine alike).

*AI evaluation harnesses* (HELM, the LM Evaluation Harness, BIG-bench, Inspect) [@liang2023helm; @biderman2024lessons; @srivastava2023bigbench; @aisi2024inspect] and agentic benchmarks [@zhou2024webarena; @xie2024osworld; @mialon2024gaia] standardize scoring, but some audits find that what was run is unrecoverable from what was reported [@burnell2023rethink; @reuel2024betterbench], and none extends to a human cohort or publication figures understandable to many audiences of a research paper.

*Agents as participants.* A fast-growing literature administers psychology experiments to language models [@binz2023gpt3; @codaforno2024cogbench; @aher2023llms; @argyle2023silicon; @webb2023analogical; @binz2025centaur] under the banner of machine psychology [@rahwan2019machine; @hagendorff2024machinepsych], yet each study re-implements a prompting harness and matches human and model administration by hand. Methodological critiques [@ivanova2025cognitive; @dillion2023replace; @lin2025fallacies] and a consensus reporting checklist [@feuerriegel2026guidellm] now demand exactly what no artifact provides, a pinned, shareable, executable record of how the experiment was administered. The same requirement appears in clinical research and the wet lab [@cdisc_odm; @ich2025m11; @beal2022labop], each formalizing one dimension, the regulatory document, the lab procedure, or the analysis plan, none an executable experiment whose subject may, unknowingly, be a person or an artificial agent.

Across these families the same limitations recur: (1) a representation is machine-facing or human-facing but rarely both; (2) experimental details stay informal during planning and execution; (3) records of what happened cover the code that ran but not the experimental decisions around it (who was eligible, how they were allocated, why data was excluded); (4) the experiment specifications that do exist cover only a few tasks, stimuli, or agents; and no artifact aligns the scientist, participant, engineer, ethics board, funding agency, reviewer, and, increasingly, the AI evaluator. No single representation spans the full study lifecycle in a form that all of them can read, validate, and execute (Figure 1).

## Desiderata for a study specification language

A notation that closes the process gap, and so specifies an experimental study end to end, must satisfy several requirements at once. We state these requirements as seven desiderata. (R1) *A single source of truth*: one artifact serves every audience, so the views projected from it cannot drift apart. (R2) *Executable, not merely descriptive*: the specification runs, not only documents. (R3) *Understandable to every audience without code*: an ethics board, a reviewer, or a collaborator can read it without programming. (R4) *Grounded in standards*: the artifact remains valid in a widely used standard notation and usable by already available tools that do not know the domain-specific vocabulary. (R5) *Process and data on one artifact*: the procedure and the data it produces are specified together. (R6) *Extensible without forking*: new domains and concepts plug in, not through changes to the core. (R7) *Executor agnostic*: who or what performs the protocol is a runtime decision, not a property of the specification. @tbl-requirements maps each desideratum to where the suggested solution, Studyflow, meets it.

## BPMN as a foundation

Meeting these desiderata is a language design problem. Experimental cognitive science meets the criteria for a domain-specific language (DSL): recurring structural patterns across studies, expert users who would benefit from a familiar notation rather than general-purpose code, and no language that already covers the whole study lifecycle [@mernik2005dsl]. Rather than invent a new notation, we extend an established one that researchers, engineers, and reviewers already recognize.

Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) is a mature graphical language for processes, standardized by ISO [@white2004introduction] and proven where an under-specified process carries real cost, in healthcare, finance, and logistics. We borrow that operational rigor for the experimental process in cognitive science. BPMN provides what scientific workflows need (events, activities, sub-processes, gateways, data objects, sequence and data flows, and choreography), an established tooling ecosystem (`bpmn-js`, Camunda Modeler, and many visualization tools), and a standard serialization, BPMN 2.0 XML, that outlives any single tool. It has already reached research and clinical study settings: ProjectFlow lets investigators build point-of-care workflows directly in BPMN 2.0 [@dhond2021projectflow], and the UK Neurosciences Center has used BPMN to map patient journeys and the data repositories they feed [@knight2024visualizing], so the choice of host notation rests on demonstrated use rather than analogy alone. Building on a graphical standard is itself a bet: whether, when, and why visual diagrams beat text is an open empirical question [@moody2009physics; @larkin1987diagram; @figl2017comprehension].

More specifically, we build our domain-specific notation on two of BPMN's extension mechanisms, `extensionElements` and namespaced attributes [@magnani2009bpdmn]. The same mechanisms are used to extend the BPMN core in many other domains [@zarour2019; @braun2014classification]; experimental cognitive science is the gap they leave. Two design decisions bound the cost of this choice for a researcher who does not know BPMN. First, an author sees and edits domain views (cognitive task, questionnaire, randomization gateway), so BPMN's generic vocabulary stays under the surface rather than in front of the user. Second, we do not delegate execution to a third-party BPMN engine, since surveys find that most engines claiming BPMN 2.0 compliance do not run the execution format [@geiger2016bpmn]; instead we execute a defined subset natively, with its semantics fixed in the Studyflow specification (Materials and methods). What BPMN contributes is therefore not an execution engine but three things a purpose-built notation would have to reinvent: a standard control-flow vocabulary with worked-out semantics, a serialization that outlives any one tool, and an extension mechanism that keeps the diagrams valid in the wider BPMN ecosystem. The rest of the paper shows how Studyflow meets these desiderata.

# The Studyflow notation

Studyflow notation represents an entire study as a single diagram: a typed directed graph (realized as a BPMN 2.0 Process) that holds together the roles named above, protocol, runnable experiment, analysis specification, and publication figure. The tooling projects a view from that one source for each audience (see Views). A reviewer reads it as a diagram, the runner app walks it node by node, the analysis code is a handful of nodes inside it, and the published CONSORT figure is a projection of it. @tbl-glance summarizes the building blocks of a Studyflow diagram, and the example in the Results section is one such file. The rest of this section defines the notation precisely; a reader who wants the intuition first can skim it and return after the worked example in Results. The reference tooling that authors and runs the diagram is described in Supplementary Note 1.

- - Element
  - What it provides

- - Activities
  - Cognitive task, questionnaire, instruction, rest, and video game, each a typed BPMN task

- - Gateways
  - Randomization, stratified allocation, and eligibility, alongside the standard BPMN gateways

- - Data elements
  - Datasets, schemas, tables, and time series, bound to BIDS, Psych-DS, BDM, and CSVW

- - Flows
  - Sequence flow (control) and data association (data) over one shared set of nodes

- - Data operations
  - transform, map, flatMap, reduce, filter, compose, and external function (`functionRef`)

- - Groups
  - Sub-processes, pools, lanes, and choreography for modularity and multi-agent structure

- - Views
  - Study (structure), Gantt (timing), Checklist (conformance), and Figure (publication rendering)

- - Extensions
  - A small core (`studyflow`, `cognitive`) plus optional extensions (`behaverse`, `omniprocess`, `datatrove`, `galea`)

## Formal definition

In plain terms, a Studyflow diagram is a set of typed boxes and arrows: the boxes and arrows are the diagram a reader sees, the types fix what each one is allowed to mean, and this section states that precisely. A Studyflow diagram is a typed, attributed directed multigraph $S = (N, E, \mathrm{src} \rightarrow \mathrm{tgt}, \tau, \lambda)$ over a schema $\Sigma$ that defines the element hierarchy. $N$ is a finite set of nodes and $E$ a finite set of edges, each running from a source $\mathrm{src}(e)$ to a target $\mathrm{tgt}(e)$ in $N$. The schema fixes a type alphabet $T$, split into node types $T_N$ (events, activities, gateways, actors, and data elements such as datasets, schemas, and stores) and edge types $T_E$. The typing $\tau: N \cup E \to T$ assigns each node a type in $T_N$ and each edge a type in $T_E$. The attribution $\lambda$ gives each element a set of attributes admissible for its type under $\Sigma$, for example the `instrument` of a cognitive task, the `probabilityFunction` of a random gateway, or the `onset` and `duration` of an activity node. Because data elements are themselves nodes of $S$, the data specification and the control flow inhabit one object (R5). @tbl-notation collects the notation used here and in later sections.

Edge type separates control flow from data flow. The sequence flow edges $E_{\mathrm{seq}}$ (those $e$ with $\tau(e)$ a sequence flow) induce the control flow graph $G_{\mathrm{ctrl}} = (N, E_{\mathrm{seq}})$. The data association edges $E_{\mathrm{assoc}}$ induce the data flow graph $G_{\mathrm{data}} = (N, E_{\mathrm{assoc}})$. The two share the node set but no edges, so one object holds (a) the order in which things happen and (b) the data each step reads and writes. Execution is a walk over $G_{\mathrm{ctrl}}$, and an analysis pipeline is a path in $G_{\mathrm{data}}$.

A diagram is *well-formed* when four conditions hold: (WF1) $\tau$ and $\lambda$ validate against $\Sigma$ and the context-free grammar relating its typed elements (Supplementary Note 1); (WF2) endpoints respect type, so every sequence flow edge runs between flow nodes (events, activities, gateways) and every data association edge joins a data element to a flow node; (WF3) $G_{\mathrm{ctrl}}$ is sound, with at least one start event and one end event and every flow node on some path from a start to an end (no dead branches); and (WF4) the serialization is valid BPMN 2.0 XML. WF1 gives the context-free and schema constraints; WF2 and WF3 are the static constraints a generic BPMN validator cannot state, and the modeler checks them by simulation before a study runs (Supplementary Note 1).

$G_{\mathrm{ctrl}}$ is directed but not acyclic, because experimental procedures contain interrupts, loops, and multi-agent exchanges that directed acyclic graphs capture only through implicit external logic; boundary events, message flows, and choreography express them natively.

*Expressiveness.* The formal object $S$ fixes not only what a diagram *is* but also what the executable language can and cannot say. Its native, runnable vocabulary expresses exactly the *finite control* experimental protocols, those whose next step is a function of the current observation and a bounded state, so that execution is a walk by a single token over $G_{\mathrm{ctrl}}$, statically checkable before a study runs. Designs that depend on accumulated history or external inference remain expressible, but only by leaving that statically checkable core. We treat the precise boundary, its examples, and its relation to the scope limit of BPMN in Materials and methods (Expressiveness and limits).

::: {#tbl-notation .list-table header-rows=1 aligns="l,l" tbl-colwidths="[36,64]"}
Studyflow formal notation, used here and reused throughout the paper.

- - Notation
  - Description

- - $S = (N, E, \mathrm{src} \rightarrow \mathrm{tgt}, \tau, \lambda)$
  - A Studyflow diagram: nodes $N$, edges $E$ directed $\mathrm{src} \rightarrow \mathrm{tgt}$, the typing $\tau$, and the attribution $\lambda$

- - $\Sigma$
  - The schema fixing the type alphabet and admissible attributes

- - $T_N$, $T_E$
  - Node types and edge types

- - $G_{\mathrm{ctrl}}$, $G_{\mathrm{data}}$
  - The control flow and data flow graphs, over the shared node set $N$

- - $\pi_p(S)$
  - A view: the projection of $S$ selected by a predicate $p$; e.g., $p \equiv \mathrm{true}$ for the Study view, $p(x) = \lambda(x).\mathit{checklist}$ for the Checklist view, $p(x) = \lambda(x).\mathit{onset} \lor \lambda(x).\mathit{duration}$ for the Gantt view, and $p(x) = \lambda(x).\mathit{visible}$ for the Figure view

- - WF1-WF4
  - The well-formedness conditions

- - $\kappa = (v, g, \sigma)$
  - An execution configuration: current node $v$, generator state $g$, opaque actor state $\sigma$

- - $\operatorname{step}$, $\operatorname{walk}$
  - The single-token transition $\kappa_{n+1} = \operatorname{step}(F, \kappa_{n}, \rho_{n})$ and the visited-node sequence it induces from the input sequence $\rho$

- - $\operatorname{rng}(s, i, \operatorname{id}(x))$
  - The random substream for element $x$, keyed by study seed $s$, subject $i$, and the element's stable identifier

- - R1-R7
  - The desiderata (@tbl-requirements)
:::


Studyflow realizes this object $S$ as a domain-specific profile of BPMN 2.0 [@white2004introduction], extended to experimental cognitive science. The diagrams stay valid BPMN 2.0 XML and open in any compliant tool, and BPMN's extension mechanism (`extensionElements`, namespaced attributes) adds the domain semantics of $T$ and $\lambda$ without breaking the underlying standard [@stroppi2011; @magnani2009bpdmn].

*What Studyflow inherits.* Studyflow reuses BPMN's full control-flow and structural vocabulary (events, activities, gateways, sequence and message flows, data objects and stores, pools and lanes, and choreography), which keep standard BPMN shapes and behave as the OMG specifies [@bpmnspec]. It leaves BPMN's serialization conventions, XML namespaces, and element identifiers untouched (see Serialization, in Materials and methods).

*What Studyflow adds.* Four areas extend BPMN with elements experimental research routinely needs. First, a root *study container* groups every other element and carries metadata for the whole study (title, version, authors, runtime). Second, domain-specific activity types specialize the generic BPMN task (cognitive tasks, questionnaires, instructions, rest, video games); each shows a distinctive icon but remains a normal BPMN task underneath. Third, domain-specific data elements bind to community schemas (BIDS [@bids], Psych-DS [@psychds], BDM [@bdm], CSVW) on top of BPMN's generic data objects. A data operation icon marks an activity with the transformation it performs (transform, map, flatMap, reduce, filter, compose) and, optionally, a `functionRef` to an external function (`scheme://ref@version` with an `arguments` block). The data flow stays visible while the work delegates to an external callable script. Fourth, additional gateways encode decision making specific to experimental design (a randomization gateway, a stratified allocation gateway, and an eligibility gateway that lists inclusion and exclusion criteria). Optional temporal attributes (onset, duration, progress) attach to activities and events, so the Gantt view derives schedules from the same diagram. @tbl-elements shows a representative subset; for the full catalog, see Supplementary Table S1.

*Extensibility.* New domains plug in by writing a schema $\Sigma'$ that extends the core $\Sigma$, adding to the type alphabet $T$ and the admissible attributes $\lambda$ without changing the core or tooling. Each new node or edge in $T'$ subclasses a core type in $T$ and carries new attributes in $\lambda'$, so the extended $S'$ is still a valid BPMN 2.0 diagram with new semantics. The current Studyflow notation splits into a small core and optional domain extensions (Figure 2): the core covers the language scaffolding and a cognitive layer, while extensions cover specific domains (see Materials and methods).

*A machine-readable specification.* The core language is defined by a versioned LinkML schema [@moxon2025linkml] that the tooling reads (Materials and methods). Listing 1 gives the schema for the study container and a cognitive task: a `CognitiveTask` specializes a BPMN activity, requires an `instrument`, and carries an inline `configurations` block. Supplementary Listing S2 shows how a domain-specific gateway maps onto BPMN: a `RandomGateway` specializes a standard `bpmn:ExclusiveGateway`, so it serializes and renders as an ordinary BPMN gateway while carrying the attributes that make randomization explicit.

**Listing 1.** Studyflow language specification (LinkML excerpt; descriptions abridged). The schema fixes element types, required attributes, and validation rules independently of any tool.

```yaml
Study:
  class_uri: bpmn:Process
  tree_root: true
  attributes:
    name:
      range: string
      required: true
    version:
      range: string
    authors:
      range: string
      multivalued: true
    runtime:
      range: RuntimeEnum

CognitiveTask:
  is_a: bpmn:Activity        # a specialized BPMN activity
  class_uri: cognitive:CognitiveTask
  attributes:
    instrument:                      # psychopy, jspsych, labjs, ...
      range: string
      required: true
    configurations:                  # instrument-specific, inline YAML
      range: YAMLString
```


## Views: Study, Gantt, Checklist, and Figure

Each visual view is a *projection* of the formal study object. Given a predicate $p$ over elements, the view $\pi_p(S)$ is the subset of $S$ induced by $\{x \in N \cup E : p(x)\}$, carrying some attributes $\lambda(x)$ unchanged and discarding the rest.

*Consistency.* A projection only discards; it never adds or rewrites, so any element kept by two views carries the same identity and attributes in both, and editing $S$ updates every $\pi_p(S)$ at once. The views are consistent by construction with the single source of truth (R1), and one `.studyflow` diagram renders in multiple ways, each suited to a different stakeholder (Figure 3).

The four suggested views in Figure 3 are four such predicates, specified formally in @tbl-notation: the Study view keeps everything; the Gantt view keeps elements carrying an `onset` or `duration` and places them on a time axis; the Checklist view keeps elements carrying a `checklist` attribute; and the Figure view keeps the visible elements, while its exported file still embeds $S$ as metadata so a published figure stays runnable (see "Figure view", below).

*Study view.* The default rendering is a BPMN-like graph showing every element and connection, in order; it serves methodology sections, reviewers checking logical structure, and developers setting up workflows.

*Gantt view.* A Gantt-like rendering places elements that carry timing along a time axis. BPMN has timer events but no native representation of duration, onset, or progress, so Studyflow adds these as optional attributes (*onset*, *duration*, *progress*), and uses BPMN pools and lanes to group rows; milestones are elements with onset but zero duration. The same mechanism scales from trial-level timing (stimulus duration, ITI, response window) to study-level scheduling (visit schedule, follow-ups), and suits trial slides, longitudinal studies, and schedules of enrolment and assessment as in SPIRIT [@spirit2013].

*Checklist view.* This task-oriented view flattens the diagram into a list of items and status, drawn from an optional `checklist` attribute on every element. It supports two use cases: *running studies day to day* (what is next, what is done) and *adhering to reporting guidelines* (CONSORT, SPIRIT, STROBE, PRISMA, and CARE), where guideline items map to the elements that satisfy them, so a study can be audited without leaving the diagram.

**Figure view.** The Figure view renders a diagram as a publication-ready image in which annotations on each element decide what is shown or hidden. A manuscript figure usually needs a curated subset of the full diagram, such as the protocol without the data layer, or a single highlighted path through a branch. Rather than redraw by hand, an author styles elements to show or hide and exports the curated image (e.g., in SVG or PNG formats). The exported image embeds the complete `.studyflow` source as metadata, so a deposited figure is the runnable file itself rather than a picture of the study; a reader can open the image in any conformant tool and re-run it. Note that journal production pipelines typically re-encode figures and strip embedded metadata, so for published articles the same guarantee comes from shipping a supplementary `.studyflow`. Because the visibility annotations live in the same file as the diagram, the figure stays valid BPMN and tied to the study it represents.

A specification is credible only if something runs it. A reference web application (MIT licensed) serves as a modeler that authors, validates, and exports diagrams, and a runner that walks a human participant or an artificial agent through a diagram node by node, behind one interface (see Supplementary materials).

# Results

The purpose of this worked example is to demonstrate the notation end to end: that one file enrolls, runs, excludes, and analyzes a heterogeneous actor cohort through a single interface. It is not to rank models as a benchmark. This section follows one study from protocol to publication: a cognitive benchmark in which a cohort of artificial agents performs a battery of six cognitive tasks over many runs, each agent allocated to a self-paced or a time-pressured path, with human participants as a validation and feasibility anchor that the same file administers behind one interface. We ask where different agents land relative to chance level and to one another, and relative to the human performance. The agent cohort table (@tbl-agents) describes the families of agents, and the battery table (@tbl-battery) describes the six cognitive tasks. The same `.studyflow` file is the input at every stage (see Data availability).

Across the six tasks, does each agent family perform above chance, and how do the trait and time-pressure manipulations move response accuracy within a family? Agreement is an equivalence test on accuracy between experimental conditions. Divergence is how well a classifier separates trials of two conditions, scored as AUC against an empirical chance level (see "Measure agreement" and "Measure divergence", below). Both measures are fixed in the protocol before the study runs. The human participants supply a descriptive reference band, not a comparison group.

Each agent is allocated to a self-paced or a time-pressured path, with task order randomized per subject within the path. Time pressure means different strategies across families of agents: an enforced response window for humans, and a deadline in the prompt for language models. So the contrast between conditions (i.e., paths in the studyflow diagram) is valid only within a family of agents.

## Design

We give the study the structure of a randomized controlled trial, following the CONSORT guidelines (the Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials, which prescribe how participants flow through a trial from enrollment to analysis). The protocol carries what a registered study needs, including consent, eligibility screening, and random allocation to the two conditions. The protocol file (an SVG image with embedded studyflow) is deposited on OSF [TODO: OSF link].

In current practice the document trail of such a study is scattered: a registry entry, a PDF for ethics approval, a recruitment system, and a CONSORT flow diagram drawn at write-up, none of them a machine-readable view of the others [@moher2012; @rennie2001; @hopewell2025consort].

We start from the CONSORT 2025 reference diagram. Figure 4 compares different ways of plotting CONSORT: (a) the standard CONSORT 2025 reference flow as published by the CONSORT group, (b) a Studyflow reproduction encoded with the same labels and pathways, and (c) an annotated contrast between the traditional text-and-boxes treatment (i.e., CONSORT for reporting, right) and the same flow encoded with boundary error events (i.e., CONSORT for execution, left).

The key difference between the traditional figure (Figure 4, panel c, right) and the executable encoding (Figure 4, panel c, left) is how participant attrition is represented. In the traditional figure, each "Excluded / Did not receive / Lost to follow-up / Discontinued" box sits beside the activities as an annotation, and readers must infer that these counts subtract from the main flow. In the executable representation, attrition is encoded as a *boundary error event* attached to the activity that participants left from. Exclusion at screening leaves the eligibility gateway, non-receipt of intervention leaves the two allocation tasks, loss to follow-up and discontinuation leave the follow-up tasks, and exclusion from analysis leaves the analysis tasks. Each event ends in an *error end event* (a standard BPMN event). This has three consequences. First, the diagram's topology now matches the runnable trial's, so a participant lost during follow-up exits along an edge that starts at the follow-up activity itself, not a side annotation. Second, and most important, the attrition counts are values the same diagram accumulates as the study runs. The file is deposited at registration with those counts empty, and the runner writes them onto the error end events (as attributes, $\lambda$) as participants leave; the registered plan and the as-run report are then one diagram at two points in its life, differing only in the values that arrived meanwhile (Listing 3). Attrition is just one such value: any element can hold others that fill in on arrival, from a per-condition enrollment count to a completion timestamp. A tool can then check that the counts an author fills in stay internally consistent (inflow equal to outflow plus attrition at each activity), but this is bookkeeping on the author's numbers, not a claim that they are correct. Third, the boundary error event is BPMN's standard primitive for interrupts, inheriting its execution semantics for exception handling [@bpmnspec; @dijkman2008semantics].

In the studyflow file, each attrition is stored in an end event whose count is a typed attribute:

```xml
...
<bpmn2:boundaryEvent id="Dropout" attachedToRef="FollowUpActivity">
  <bpmn2:outgoing>Flow_Dropout_Excluded</bpmn2:outgoing>
  <bpmn2:errorEventDefinition id="ErrorDef_Dropout" />
</bpmn2:boundaryEvent>
<bpmn2:endEvent id="Dropout_End" name="Dropped out (n=...)">
  <bpmn2:extensionElements>
    <studyflow:attrition count="..." />
  </bpmn2:extensionElements>
  <bpmn2:errorEventDefinition errorRef="ErrorDef_Dropout" />
</bpmn2:endEvent>
...
```

The diagram carries domain semantics alongside the BPMN structure. The enrollment start event references the consent participants see, so an ethics board approves the same consent that a runner app renders when it reaches this node. The screening task carries a checklist that drives the *Checklist* view (e.g., the demographics, medical history, and items from the CONSORT template). The eligibility and randomization gateways carry decision makings. Each cognitive task declares its own parameters (e.g., for the N-back: the N, stimulus duration, inter-trial interval, and trials per block); and the allocation, follow-up, and analysis tasks carry checklists describing protocol obligations. Together, these layers render as the CONSORT diagram while being runnable for data collection and serving as a checklist.

Where CONSORT structures the *report*, SPIRIT structures the *plan*. The same study also renders as a SPIRIT 2025 schedule of enrolment and assessment, its checklist items mapping onto the Gantt view [@chan2025spirit; @spirit2013]. A SPIRIT plan and a CONSORT report are then the same file at two points in its lifecycle: the schedule before randomization, and the flow diagram with attrition counts written into the boundary events once the study has run.

CONSORT and SPIRIT were written for human trials, and routing an artificial agent cohort through the same flow is notational rather than a claim about the agents (see Discussion). The example here shows that the same flow collects data from an artificial agent wherever it collects data from a human participant.

## Enroll and run

*One interface, many actors.* The runner app can now walk the diagram node by node, administering every actor, human or artificial, through one interface. Per trial it sends the stimulus, the allowed responses, the timing constraint, and where needed rendered frames (i.e., screenshot images). It records the response and, where applicable, the response time. Each actor keeps its own state locally, a participant's session, an agent's policy, a recurrent hidden state, or a language model's context.

This example study fills the runner with two kinds of actor behind the one interface, plus a uniform random baseline for chance level. The human runner renders each trial in the GUI and blocks until a person responds; language model agents receive the trial with trait and instruction prompts, and vision models also read the rendered screenshots [@schulzebuschoff2025visual; @tangtartharakul2026deficits]. Response time is interpretable only where the actor produces it as behavior: measured for humans, elapsed latency or token budget for language models (@tbl-agents).

If an actor replies outside the allowed response options, the runner records the raw reply and flags the trial as missing; no response is imputed. A run whose rate of failed trials exceeds 20% on any task exits through the boundary error event of the CONSORT and is counted in the participant flow, so agent dropout goes through the same edge as human loss to follow-up. <!-- REVIEWER: 20% is a registered placeholder threshold; confirm before submission. These failed-trial counts are the agent arm's run-time values written back into the diagram (the same mechanism as CONSORT attrition); report them as such. --> Failed trials are typed by failure mode (invalid, timeout, refusal), reported in @tbl-agents. The full runner configuration is pinned to every run (Materials and methods) [@ivanova2025cognitive; @lampinen2024content].

*The cognitive battery.* The study administers six cognitive tasks spanning working memory, attention, processing speed, fluid reasoning, and set-shifting (@tbl-battery). Each task runs multiple trials per subject, and humans and agents are compared only at the task level. The N-back serves as the worked example below, and the other tasks use the same machinery. To show the notation is not tied to our own task library, the battery also includes one external, non-Behaverse Flanker task referenced from a public jsPsych library through a `functionRef` (Listing 2), administered through the same runner.

::: {#tbl-battery .list-table header-rows=1 aligns="l,l,l" tbl-colwidths="[26,24,50]"}
The selected cognitive tasks from the Behaverse battery [@behaverse] and the construct each is historically associated with. The construct is a historical label, not a measurement claim.

- - Task

  - Reference

- - N-back

- - Digit span
  - Working memory

- - Multiple-object tracking

*Enroll, allocate, and follow up.* We authored the battery as one diagram that orchestrates the four CONSORT stages: enrollment through consent and baseline questionnaires, an eligibility gateway, randomized allocation to the self-paced and time-pressured paths, and follow-up through the six tasks. Each task is itself a set of trial blocks that common methodology prose may flatten but the diagram keeps explicit (a tutorial, a practice, and the test blocks). Once loaded into a study runner app, the diagram is checked for required parameters and then walked one node at a time (Supplementary Figure S3). Randomness policy (i.e., a seed) fixes the subject's path, task order, stimulus order, and every randomized branch. Each agent runs $k = 30$ times per condition under predefined parameters, and its performance is reported aggregated over multiple runs. The value of $k$ and the failed-trial exclusion threshold (the 20% rule above) are prespecified in the registered `.studyflow` file, fixed before any run rather than chosen after seeing the data. <!-- REVIEWER: k = 30 is a registered placeholder value; confirm or adjust before submission. With it fixed, the prespecification claim in "Measure agreement" now holds. --> The same flow runs for artificial agents and the human participants alike.

*Encoding the trials.* Figure 5 places the traditional slide figure of the N-back next to the studyflow equivalent. The slide is intuitive but underspecified: timing values often live only in the caption, the trial-block boundary stays implicit, and decisions like "what counts as a correct match" are buried in analysis code. Studyflow encodes the trial as an explicit subprocess (a stimulus activity, a boundary timer for the response window, a second for the inter-trial interval, and target and non-target branches labeled by annotations and a code reference), which compresses into a single cognitive task whose parametrization declares the N, trial count, stimulus type, duration, and interval. Each trial is logged in a standard data format (BDM [@bdm]) whose schema fixes the CSV columns and whose diagram fixes their use.

*Listing 2.* Two tasks from the worked study serialized in one `.studyflow` file (BPMN 2.0 XML; stimulus streams truncated for display). The first is a native Behaverse N-back: a standard `bpmn:Task` carrying a `behaverse:task` extension that declares the N in N-back, the stimulus stream, and the timing. The second is an external, non-Behaverse Flanker task administered through the same runner. It touches only the core `cognitive` layer and names its implementation with a `functionRef` to a versioned jsPsych library (`scheme://ref@version`), so it depends on no Behaverse component while remaining a first-class node of the same diagram.

```xml
<bpmn2:task id="Task_NB" name="N-back (digits)">
  <bpmn2:extensionElements>
    <behaverse:task scene="NB">
      <cognitive:configurations>Blocks:
        NB2:
          Parameters:
            NValue: 2
            Feature: Digits
            Streams:
              - StimulusValue:
                  Sequence:
                    Type: Ordered
                    Values: [3, 1, 2, 1, 3, 2, 3, 2, 1, 2, 3, 1]
            StreamSize: 12
            StimulusDisplayDuration: 0.5
            InterStimulusInterval: 1.5
      Timelines:
        Main:
          blocks:
            - name: NB2
      </cognitive:configurations>
    </behaverse:task>
  </bpmn2:extensionElements>
  <bpmn2:incoming>Flow_B_Start_NB</bpmn2:incoming>
  <bpmn2:outgoing>Flow_NB_DS</bpmn2:outgoing>
</bpmn2:task>

<bpmn2:task id="Task_FL" name="Flanker (external)">
  <bpmn2:extensionElements>
    <cognitive:cognitiveTask instrument="jspsych">
      <cognitive:functionRef>https://github.com/jspsych/jspsych-contrib@v0.4.0#flanker</cognitive:functionRef>
      <cognitive:configurations>
        n_trials: 96
        InterStimulusInterval: 0.5
      </cognitive:configurations>
    </cognitive:cognitiveTask>
  </bpmn2:extensionElements>
  <bpmn2:incoming>Flow_DS_FL</bpmn2:incoming>
  <bpmn2:outgoing>Flow_FL_End</bpmn2:outgoing>
</bpmn2:task>
```

*The agent cohort.* The registered `.studyflow` file specifies a full matrix of agents over the whole battery, crossing three factors within each path:

- *Model*: a uniform random baseline as a chance reference, several large language models served locally through Ollama, and one or more commercial vision-language models that also read the rendered screen.
- *Trait*: a baseline mode with no trait prompt, plus three personas drawn from human characterizations, namely a careful persona (a conservative decision criterion [@ratcliff2008diffusion]), a fatigued persona (intermittent attentional lapses [@robertson1997oops]), and a fast, error-prone persona (the speed-accuracy trade-off [@wickelgren1977sat]).
- *Task*: the six battery tasks.

The trait manipulation is a prompt for language models [@argyle2023silicon; @aher2023llms], read within a family; trait prompts name a disposition, never a target accuracy, so they do not steer the agreement estimate. Agents are allocated exhaustively, $k = 30$ runs per condition, a factorial rather than randomized allocation; the CONSORT allocation therefore applies only to the human participants, and the studyflow file makes that explicit rather than hiding it. The file specifies this full grid, which is itself evidence that the notation scales to a realistic study. What we execute here is a minimal but sufficient subset of it, one language model, one vision language model, and the chance baseline, on two tasks (the N-back and the Flanker) under one trait contrast and both paths. That slice exercises every stage of the pipeline (enrollment, allocation, the failed-trial exclusion, the agreement and divergence tests, and the CONSORT figure) across more than one actor family, which is what demonstrates the notation. The remaining models, traits, and tasks are specified in the same file and run by the same machinery.

@tbl-agents reports accuracy, the rate of failed trials, and response time where it is a behavioral measure, for every executed condition, and Figure 6 shows these profiles across the two demonstrated tasks against the two-participant human anchor band [TODO: values from the runs]. <!-- REVIEWER: payload exhibit for R7. The executed slice (baseline + one open-weight LLM + one commercial VLM; two tasks, native N-back and external Flanker; baseline+one trait; both paths) demonstrates cross-family completion and exercises every pipeline stage. The registered file specifies the full grid; remaining cells run by the same machinery. Fill this table and Figure 6 from the executed slice before submission. --> Rather than rank many models on a single task, a choice that itself may move rankings [@dehghani2021lottery], we vary the diagram (task, response window, trait) and measure a cohort of agents over a battery of parametrically related items, the design that recent AI evaluation literature has begun to call for [@wang2026psychometrics; @bean2025construct]. The nearest existing artifacts make the differentiation concrete: CogBench scores many language models on seven fixed paradigms behind one harness [@codaforno2024cogbench], and Psych-101 transcribes 160 experiments into text [@binz2025centaur]. Here the same protocol administers both, and the task battery re-parameterizes from the diagram.
